extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduates and graduate students (and researchers) studying algebraic geometry; readers of Vakil's Foundations of Algebraic Geometry
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and tests for (relative) smoothness and regularity of schemes (Jacobian criterion, base-change checks, tangent space descriptions), geometric consequences (tangent planes, Bertini), and equivalent characterizations of dimension-1 regular/local rings (DVR/UFD/PID/valuation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Jacobian criterion for smoothness/regularity
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the Jacobian matrix of defining equations: smoothness/regularity at a point can be checked by the rank/corank of the Jacobian. For a finite type k-scheme X of pure dimension d over an algebraically closed field, regularity at closed points can be shown via the Jacobian criterion by checking that the corank of the Jacobian is d at the closed points of X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the Jacobian matrix ((12.1.6.1) style) evaluated at the point; singular closed points for a hypersurface f=0 correspond to simultaneous vanishing of f and all partials ∂f/∂xi. The criterion is readily checked on affine covers (see Exercise 12.2.I and Exercise 12.2.D). Be mindful of characteristic issues (e.g., df/dx may vanish in positive characteristic even when the ring is a field).

rubrics_metrics.name: Smoothness-Regularity Comparison Theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: Relationship between smoothness and regularity: (a) If k is perfect, every regular finite type k-scheme is smooth over k. (b) Every smooth k-scheme is regular (no hypothesis on perfection).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part (a) is proved later (Exercise 21.3.D); part (b) follows from étale-local structure (every smooth variety locally admits an étale morphism to A^n_k) and the fact that étale morphisms preserve regularity at points (see Exercise 25.2.D). Caution: regularity need not imply smoothness when the base field is not perfect — see explicit counterexample X = Spec k[x]/(x^p - u) over k = F_p(u).

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution: regularity does not imply smoothness over non-perfect fields
rubrics_metrics.description: Regular schemes/rings can fail to be smooth over the base if the base field is not perfect. Example: k = F_p(u), X = Spec k[x]/(x^p - u) is a field and hence regular, but the Jacobian criterion fails so X is not smooth over k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This illustrates smoothness is a relative notion depending on the base field; always check base-field hypotheses (perfect vs non-perfect) when replacing 'regular' by 'smooth'. Additional examples: curves like y^2 − x^p + u giving regular but non-smooth closed points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check regularity at closed points by separable base change
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is a finite type k-scheme of pure dimension n and p ∈ X is a closed point with residue field k', separable over k of degree d, then X_k := X ×_k k̄ (or appropriate separable extension) is regular at all preimages p1,...,pd of p if and only if X is regular at p.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof strategy (Exercise 12.2.O): reduce to affine case Spec A; tensor exact sequences with k̄ (field extensions preserve exactness for vector spaces); compare dimensions of Zariski tangent spaces: sum_i dim_k(T_{X_k,pi}) = d · dim_{k'}(T_{X,p}). For Galois extensions one can use transitive Gal(k'/k)-action to deduce regularity at one preimage suffices. Use this to check regularity at closed points by base changing to a field where computations are easier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tangent plane/line via linearized defining equations
rubrics_metrics.description: At a k-valued regular point a of a scheme X ⊂ A^n_k cut out by equations f1,...,fr, the tangent d-plane T_pX is given by the r linear equations Σ_j (∂fi/∂x_j)(a) · (x_j − a_j) = 0. This description is independent of the choice of defining equations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jacobian criterion ensures these linear equations cut out a d-plane when X is regular of dimension d. This matches the multivariable calculus notion of tangent plane without ε–δ arguments. Use this to compute tangent lines/planes explicitly (Exercises 12.3.I, 12.3.J) and to check invariance under automorphisms of A^n or P^n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Euler/Jacobian test for singular points of projective hypersurfaces
rubrics_metrics.description: For a projective hypersurface f = 0 in P^n_k (k algebraically closed), the singular closed points correspond to the common zeros of f and all partial derivatives ∂f/∂x_i. If deg f is not divisible by char k, one can use the Euler relation (deg f) · f = Σ_i x_i (∂f/∂x_i) to reduce checks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Euler identity to relate f and the partials when char k does not divide deg f; this can simplify singularity checks. Warning: be careful in small characteristics (e.g., char k dividing deg f) when applying the Euler reduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Line contained in tangent plane iff intersection multiplicity ≥ 2
rubrics_metrics.description: For X a degree d hypersurface in P^n_k and L a line not contained in X, if L meets X with multiplicity at least 2 at a k-valued regular point p, then L is contained in the tangent plane to X at p.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an application of the Jacobian/tangent-plane description; geometrically: multiple intersection at a smooth point forces the line to lie in the linear tangent space. Useful for visualization and multiplicity computations (Exercise 12.3.K).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bertini's Theorem (smooth hyperplane sections)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X ⊂ P^n_k is a smooth subvariety (k algebraically closed), then there exists a nonempty dense open subset U of the dual projective space P^n∨_k such that for every hyperplane H corresponding to a closed point of U that does not contain any component of X, the scheme H ∩ X is k-smooth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategy: define the incidence/‘bad’ variety Z = {(p ∈ X, H ∈ P^n∨) : p ∈ H and H∩X is singular at p or H contains X}, show fibers over p are projective spaces of dimension n−d−1 so dim Z ≤ n−1, hence image in P^n∨ is a proper closed subset; complement is open dense. Consequences: general degree-d hyperplane sections are smooth; general hyperplanes meet X transversely. Variants exist removing algebraically closed hypothesis (Exercise 12.4.A) or weakening hypotheses (finite singular set, local complete intersection embedding).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dual projective space and dual variety
rubrics_metrics.description: The dual projective space P^n∨ parametrizes hyperplanes in P^n. The image of the incidence variety Z in P^n∨ is the dual variety of X; for a smooth irreducible X the dual is expected to be a hypersurface of P^n∨ (dim Z = n−1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The algebraic description via appended Jacobian column captures the condition that H intersects X singularly at p. The dual of a hyperplane is the corresponding point in P^n∨; the dual of the dual returns X under appropriate hypotheses (classical duality). Exercises explore examples (smooth conics, tangency counts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Regularity preserved under polynomial extension (A^1-extension)
rubrics_metrics.description: If (B,n) is a regular local ring then localizations of B[x] at primes over n are regular local rings; in particular, if X is a regular (locally Noetherian) scheme then so is X × A^1, and A^n_k is regular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposition 12.3.6: analyze two cases for primes of B[x] over n: (i) fiber A^1_k (p = nB[x]) where height equals dim B and generators lift, (ii) closed point of the fiber corresponding to irreducible polynomial g(x), where height is dim B + 1. Use Krull's Height Theorem and generation of maximal ideals to show regularity of localizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalent characterizations of Noetherian local dimension-1 regular rings (DVR equivalences)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a Noetherian local ring (A,m) of dimension 1 the following are equivalent: (a) A is regular; (b) m is principal; (c) every ideal is of the form m^n or (0); (d) A is a PID (in this context); (e) A is a discrete valuation ring (DVR); (f) A is a unique factorization domain; (g) A is integrally closed in its fraction field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Nakayama's Lemma to show (a)⇒(b). From a principal maximal ideal (uniformizer t) every nonzero element is t^n·(unit), giving valuation v and DVR structure. Conversely, DVR⇒Noetherian regular local dim 1. Show equivalences by checking ideals structure, valuations, and integrality arguments (Theorems 12.5.1, 12.5.4, 12.5.6, 12.5.8). Exercises provide concrete examples (Z, k[x]_(x), Z[i], p-adic valuation rings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular local rings are integral domains; uniqueness of irreducible component through a regular point
rubrics_metrics.description: If (A,m,k) is a regular local ring of dimension n then A is an integral domain (Theorem 12.2.13). Consequently, for a Noetherian scheme X, if p is a regular point then only one irreducible component of X passes through p (Exercise 12.2.J).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by induction on dimension using regularity of hypersurface quotients and Nakayama-type arguments: choose f ∈ m \, m^2 to reduce dimension and use properties of minimal prime ideals. Geometric intuition: smooth points are locally irreducible.
